citation: Glessner House Museum, 'Queer, Quaint, and . . . Dutch??', The Story of a House (blog), 8 June 2015.
author: Glessner House Museum
locator: The post's introduction (the clipping's source and dating) and its closing 'NOTES', the paragraph on Richardson's courtyard design. The 1887 article it transcribes is its own record, glessner_scrapbook_1887_queer_house_clipping.
rights_note: A museum's blog post, cited in words only; nothing is copied from it.
access_notes: Read 2026-11-07 (T-3488) from the live page in full (HTML 101,498 bytes, sha256 926d33a85463b33f813022b9a69fe825ba1ea8cf79b90ba2dff44cedea2b1dbe).
note: Read, the introduction: the article 'is found pasted in the Glessners' scrapbook. The newspaper in which it was published is not identified, but it appears to date to the latter part of 1887, just before the Glessners moved into their home.' The notes: 'Richardson's original design for the Glessner courtyard did feature a fountain and elaborate gardens; these were eliminated in later modifications, presumably due to the fact the Glessners spent their summers in New Hampshire.' Later scholarship by the house's own museum: it gives no date for the change and cites no document for it, and its 'presumably' is the author's reasoning.
what_it_supplies: the museum's statement that the fountain and elaborate gardens of Richardson's courtyard design were eliminated in later modifications
that the 1887 clipping's newspaper is unidentified and its date is the museum's estimate
what_it_does_not_supply: when the fountain and gardens were dropped, or what the court held instead
a period source for the elimination
